q: Environment is everything that is around us. It can be living (biotic) or non-living (______).
e: The textbook defines environment as including both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components.

q: The four major components of the environment together are known as the ______.
e: Figure 6.1 and the accompanying text state that the four components—hydrosphere, lithosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere—together form the ecosphere.

q: The hydrosphere includes all ______ such as lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, and oceans.
e: The textbook explicitly states that the hydrosphere includes all water bodies like lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, and oceans.

q: Lithosphere mainly contains soil, earth rocks, mountains, etc., and is divided into three layers: crust, mantle, and ______.
e: According to section 6.1.1, the lithosphere is divided into crust, mantle, and core (outer and inner).

q: The cover of air that envelopes the Earth is known as the ______.
e: Section 6.1.1 defines the atmosphere as the thin layer of air enveloping the Earth.

q: The biosphere is otherwise known as the ______.
e: The textbook states that the biosphere is 'otherwise known as the life layer'.

q: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and also with the surrounding ______.
e: Section 6.1.2 defines an ecosystem as involving interactions between organisms and their physical environment.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a terrestrial ecosystem in the textbook?
e: Coral reefs are part of marine ecosystems; rainforests and grasslands are explicitly listed as terrestrial ecosystems.

q: Freshwater ecosystems comprise about ______ of the Earth's surface.
e: The textbook states that freshwater ecosystems make up 1.8% of the Earth's surface.

q: Marine ecosystems are the ______ ecosystem of the Earth.
e: Section 6.1.2 describes marine ecosystems as 'the largest ecosystem of the Earth'.

q: In an ecosystem, green plants that photosynthesise to produce food are called ______.
e: Producers are defined as green plants that photosynthesise to produce food.

q: Animals that eat plants or other animals are known as ______.
e: The textbook defines consumers as animals that eat plants or other animals.

q: Organisms that break down dead material and help to recycle nutrients are called ______.
e: Decomposers are described as organisms that break down dead material and recycle nutrients; they are also termed reducers.

q: Abiotic factors include all of the following EXCEPT ______.
e: Predation is a biotic factor; temperature and soil pH are abiotic factors listed in the text.

q: Biotic factors include all of the following EXCEPT ______.
e: Salinity is an abiotic factor; the others are biotic interactions mentioned in the textbook.

q: All the organisms of a particular species found in an ecosystem at a certain time form a ______.
e: The textbook defines a population as all organisms of a particular species in an ecosystem at a given time.

q: The populations of all species found in an ecosystem at a particular time form the ______.
e: A community is defined as the collection of all populations of different species in an ecosystem at a given time.

q: In a food chain, the arrow (→) means ______.
e: The textbook explicitly states that in a food chain, the arrow means 'is eaten by'.

q: The different stages in a food chain (producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer) are called ______.
e: These stages are defined as trophic levels in section 6.2.1.

q: A food web shows feeding relationships with ______.
e: The textbook explains that a food web illustrates feeding relationships across different food chains in an ecosystem.

q: Pollution is the effect of ______ changes in our surroundings that have harmful effects on plants, animals and human beings.
e: The textbook defines pollution as resulting from 'undesirable changes' in the environment.

q: A substance which causes pollution is called a ______.
e: The term 'pollutant' is used in the textbook to describe any substance causing pollution.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as one of the seven major types of pollution?
e: The seven types listed are air, water, land, light, noise, thermal, and radioactive pollution; 'chemical pollution' is not separately listed.

q: Air pollution can be caused by all of the following EXCEPT ______.
e: Photosynthesis is a natural process that does not cause air pollution; car exhaust and industries are listed as causes.

q: Water pollution causes diseases such as dysentery, typhoid, jaundice and ______.
e: The textbook lists fever among the diseases caused by water pollution.

q: Land pollution leads to soil erosion, shift of animals' habitats and adverse effects on the health of ______.
e: The text states land pollution adversely affects both animals and humans.

q: Noise pollution is caused by machines, transport, construction sites, etc., and can cause ______.
e: High blood pressure is listed among the health effects of noise pollution.

q: Thermal pollution is the degradation of water quality by any process that changes ______.
e: Thermal pollution is defined as changing ambient water temperature.

q: Light pollution includes electronic billboards, night sports grounds, street lights, and ______.
e: Residential areas are listed as sources of artificial light contributing to light pollution.

q: Radioactive pollution is caused by the emission of high energy particles or radioactive substances from ______.
e: The textbook identifies nuclear weapons and nuclear fuel as sources of radioactive pollution.

q: A nutrient cycle is a repeated pathway of a particular nutrient from the physical environment to living organisms and back to the ______.
e: The definition specifies the cycle returns the nutrient 'back to the environment'.

q: The six main nutrient cycles include carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorous, and ______.
e: Sulphur is listed as the sixth main nutrient cycle.

q: Nitrogen gas constitutes ______ of the atmosphere.
e: The textbook states nitrogen gas makes up 78% of the atmosphere.

q: The enzyme that catalyses the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia is called ______.
e: Nitrogenase is the enzyme produced by nitrogen-fixing bacteria for this reaction.

q: Rhizobium forms a mutualistic association with the roots of ______.
e: Rhizobium is specified to associate with legume roots.

q: Ammonification is the process by which decomposers break down organic nitrogen to produce ______.
e: Ammonification releases ammonia (and ammonium ions) from decaying matter.

q: Nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas convert ammonium ions into ______.
e: Nitrosomonas converts ammonium to nitrites; Nitrobacter converts nitrites to nitrates.

q: Denitrification converts nitrates into ______.
e: Denitrifying bacteria reduce nitrates to nitrogen gas ($N_2$).

q: Phosphorus is a component of biological molecules such as RNA, DNA, phospholipids, and ______.
e: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is listed as a key molecule containing phosphorus.

q: In the phosphorus cycle, phosphorus is released from rocks through the process of ______.
e: Weathering of phosphate-containing rocks releases phosphorus into the soil.

q: Sulphur is an essential component of many ______ and enzyme cofactors.
e: The textbook states sulphur is part of many proteins and enzyme cofactors.

q: When fossil fuels are burnt, sulphur is released as ______.
e: Burning fossil fuels releases sulphur as $SO_2$, a component of acid rain.

q: A drug is any substance that is taken into the body that alters or influences ______ in the body.
e: The textbook defines a drug as altering or influencing chemical reactions in the body.

q: Penicillin is an antibiotic used to cure bacterial infections such as pneumonia, gonorrhoea, and ______.
e: Syphilis is listed alongside pneumonia and gonorrhoea as treatable by penicillin.

q: Aspirin is a sedative drug used as a ______.
e: Aspirin is described as a painkiller that numbs pain-sensitive parts of the brain.

q: Drug abuse refers to the use of chemicals for the purpose of creating ______ on the brain.
e: The textbook defines drug abuse as using chemicals to create pleasurable effects on the brain.

q: Heroin is a strong ______.
e: Heroin is explicitly called a strong sedative in the text.

q: Withdrawal symptoms of heroin include insomnia, muscle cramps, sweating, headaches, diarrhoea, vomiting and ______.
e: Nausea is listed among the withdrawal symptoms of heroin.

q: Excessive alcohol consumption can lead to stomach ulcers, heart disease, and ______.
e: Brain damage is listed as a serious long-term effect of heavy alcohol use.

q: Tobacco smoke contains harmful substances such as nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide and ______.
e: Smoke particles are listed alongside nicotine, tar, and carbon monoxide as harmful components.

q: Smoking can lead to chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer, and increases the risk of ______.
e: Heart disease is explicitly mentioned as a risk increased by smoking.

q: If a pregnant woman smokes, the baby may be born underweight or even ______.
e: The textbook states the baby may be 'born underweight or even born dead'.
